Lottery-winner and Ferrari examples hedged as Harari's.
facts: Chapter 19 'And They Lived Happily Ever After': researchers define happiness as subjective well-being and use questionnaires on a 0-10 scale, comparing groups.
History has little research on happiness; Harari suggests people today are not significantly happier than in earlier eras.

Happiness depends less on objective conditions than on how they compare with expectations: new Ferrari wanted, used Fiat received; lottery winners end near the long-term happiness of people after a debilitating car accident.
Biochemistry as thermostat: a set level that differs by person; illustration of 6-10 settling at 8 and 3-7 settling at 5; the French Revolution changed institutions but not French biochemistry.
Kahneman's study: parenting has many unpleasant moments yet parents call children their chief source of happiness; Harari: happiness comes from seeing one's whole life as meaningful.
Nietzsche quote: 'If you have a why to live, you can bear almost any how.' Medieval life was hard but belief in an afterlife may have made it feel meaningful.
Method example: 1,000 people earning $100,000 vs 1,000 earning $50,000; money raises happiness up to a point; family and community matter more than money or health.
scene_details: a questionnaire answered on a 0-10 scale
a new Ferrari wanted and a used Fiat received
a thermostat settling at 8 or at 5
tension: Wealth and comfort grow while measured happiness may not, because happiness tracks expectations and meaning.
opening_idea: Open on the Ferrari/Fiat or the thermostat numbers.
